“MEME VALUE”
Every living, inanimate and abstract entity possesses “meme
value”. I believe that meme value permeates everything, and,
the beholder can perceive, transmit, or transform it. With the
advent of blockchain, specifically Ethereum*, we can now
build token-native memes and, thus, we are witnessing, in
real-time, how this value accrues to the source of the meme
(or doesn’t), and how the value spreads, grows and births
new memes and society norms.
WRITTEN AND ILLUSTRATED BY 67
UNLESS SPECIFIED OTHERWISE
*Ethereum - a decentralized blockchain platform that enables
the creation and execution of smart contracts and decentralized
applications (dApps), with its native cryptocurrency, Ether (ETH),
facilitating transactions and computational services on the
network. Also known as “The World Computer”.

PRELUDE / INTRO
This book is not a promotion of NFTs or crypto. It
is a record of an ongoing probe into new, networked
societies known as Nounish DAOs.
The illustrations document onchain proposals,
auctions, debates, rituals, and moments of collective
decision-making. They are artifacts from a live
system, captured mid-process, not polished in
hindsight. Over the past two years, I have used
characters and scenes as a way to compress complex
technical and social dynamics into something
observable, testable, and human.
My practice has unfolded publicly, largely through
Ethereum and the Farcaster protocol, and Lil Nouns/
Nouns, where ideas can be proposed, contested,
funded, ignored, or forked in real time. These
environments behave less like platforms and more
like self-regulating systems that produce their own
norms, aesthetics, incentives and pathologies. They
are imperfect, unfinished, and often absurd. That is
precisely why they are interesting.
The figures in this book are mostly fictional. They
are often shown pausing, reflecting, or re-evaluating,
caught in feedback loops rather than heroic poses.
The characters are Nounish, but not ordinary. The
glasses commonly associated with Nouns appear
inconsistently, sometimes omitted entirely. This is
deliberate. The logo is not the system; it is only a
symbol that points toward it.
Nouns is a headless brand. It enforces no singular
aesthetic and no official narrative. What persists
instead is an ethic that emerges through repeated
action: striving to improve shared conditions, giving
more than you take, placing collective outcomes
above individual extraction, and doing so with
sincerity and play.
Failure is informative
This book does not attempt to explain that ethic.
It observes it, where it holds, where it fails, and
where it mutates.

KATHERINE BOYLE, GENERAL PARTNER | A16Z:
When evaluating a company, one
of my favorite questions to ask is
whether it has an aesthetic.
We don’t talk about aesthetics as the highest form of brand or story or a reflection of team
cohesion, because investing on “vibes” or “look” or “mood” is very frowned upon. Even using
it as a data point is beaten out of us. But if you look at any entity that’s successful across
industries, you know its aesthetic. A singular company doesn’t just have a brand, it has an
aesthetic that dominates its culture, its people and all products that come from it, whether the
font on the wall art or the core product its selling.
It’s not just best companies. The best sports teams have an aesthetic. The best artists. The best
campaigns have strong aesthetic. And the more cohesive an aesthetic is, the more successful
and durable the culture is.
If you’re trying to decide which candidate is going to win an election, ask yourself which team
has a more cohesive and stronger aesthetic. If you’re trying to decide which company will
dominate a market, see if you can pick out the company’s people or products out of a lineup.
Numbers often lie. Narratives can be false. But it’s really, really hard to fake aesthetic. And if a
company has one early and it’s genuine, it’s often much more durable than it appears.

LIL PING, NERD | MAKE DAOS HAPPEN:
To resist the influence of “extreme statements” and viral memes, one effective approach is to
adopt a mindset similar to that of Socrates—engaging in continuous, critical questioning. This
method involves not accepting statements at face value but instead probing their meaning and
validity. For instance, if someone claims, “Investing relies on aesthetics,” you might ask:
What does “aesthetics” mean in this context?
Can you provide a clear explanation or example?
What evidence supports this claim?
If the explanation becomes increasingly vague or abstract, it may be wise to approach the
statement with skepticism and avoid internalizing or spreading it without thorough understanding.
This practice aligns with the concept of “anti-mimetic” training, which involves consciously
resisting the automatic imitation of ideas and behaviors prevalent in culture. By doing so, you
maintain autonomy over your thoughts and actions, rather than being passively influenced by
prevailing trends.
In situations where questioning others directly might be socially uncomfortable, consider
directing these inquiries inward or utilizing tools like AI to explore and analyze the ideas further.
This reflective approach helps in discerning the validity of information and prevents the uncritical
adoption of potentially misleading concepts.
Ultimately, by embracing continuous questioning and critical thinking, you empower yourself to
navigate the complex landscape of information and ideas with discernment and integrity.

Lil Nouns DAO
Where our journey begins: Lil Design Research Project (I,II,III) to pursue
research and design for Lil Nouns DAO, thus creating this book.
The underlying ethos of Lil Nouns may reflect that of Nouns, yet the meme
remains open for interpretation and largely undiscovered. Lil Nouns is a
fork of Nouns DAO, the “Wild West of Nouns”, dubbed by those within as a
social layer for Nounish culture to flourish. Participation is often described as
inclusion. In practice, it functions as selection. When the same actors repeatedly
initiate, approve, and reward activity within a system, participation ceases to
be exploratory and becomes confirmatory. The system no longer responds to
new inputs; it validates existing ones. Over time, decision-making narrows.
Novel behavior is tolerated only when it aligns with prior outcomes. Dissent is
reframed as inefficiency. Repetition is reclassified as legitimacy.
The emission curve enables faster paced growth at a more accessible price point,
yet whale-dictated floor and reserve prices have, in my view, stalled growth in
the token supply. The system continues to operate, funds continue to move and
proposals continue to execute. What disappears is not activity, but learning.
At this stage, participation serves a different function:
to signal belonging,
to recycle justification,
to maintain access.
No explicit exclusion is required.
The structure performs it automatically.
Systems like this do not fail loudly.
They persist quietly, optimized for themselves.
By the time the pattern is recognized, it has already become tradition. I have
watched many DAOs (almost Nouns) succumb to the above and hope for a
different fate at Lil Nouns DAO.
A pool of 256 available Lil Nouns exists at lilnouns.auction and are priced on a
bonding curve with a reserve price of 0.03ETH (adjustable), the 0.03ETH goes
directly to the DAO treasury and you get a token.

Lil Noun 1 – Lil Nouns Genesis and Bridge:
Lil Noun 1 is the second NFT from the Lil Nouns
collection. Uniquely, Lil Noun 1 is held within the Nouns
DAO treasury, exemplifying the tight coupling between the
two DAOs. The Lil Nouns protocol sends every 10th Lil
Noun to Nouns DAO, giving Nouns DAO an 8% stake in
Lil Nouns governance.
Provenance-wise, Lil Noun 1 served as a symbolic gift
to Nouns DAO, ensuring Nouns DAO was a stakeholder
from day one. Culturally, this NFT represents the “child
project” paying homage to their “parent”. Nouns DAO voters
immediately had influence in Lil Nouns decisions, injecting
Nouns ethos into the forked DAO. Conversely, Lil Nouns
began using funds to acquire Nouns NFTs for their treasury,
feeding back into Nouns DAO’s governance. This reciprocal

ownership (Nouns holding Lil Nouns, and Lil Nouns holding
Nouns) increases the variety of voices and cross-pollination
of ideas in both communities. As of 2025, Lil Noun 1’s
role has been solely symbolic: it stands for cultural and
governance interdependence – a meme of “DAO of DAOs”
– showing how proliferating the Nounish meme through
derivative collections can introduce new members and
behaviors (Lil Nouns attracted many who weren’t in Nouns
DAO), whilst still reinforcing the core visual identity
(Noogles and trait parity as of 2025) across the ecosystem.
That all sounds great on paper, but the reality is that
nothing has ever really been explored here and there is
definitely room for novel experiments/collaborations
between the two DAOs.
One Noun auctioned everyday, forever.

Noun 1 – The Genesis Auction (August 8th 2021)
Noun 1 was the first Noun auctioned (a fox-headed Noun)
and sold for an astonishing 613.37 ETH (≈$2.1M) to
collector xaix.eth, making it the most expensive Noun to
date. This early sale set the stage for Nouns’ meme-driven
value, as even the bid (613.37 contains “1337”) gave a nod
to crypto culture.
Culturally, Noun 1 became a symbol of Nouns DAO’s bold
beginning and the high conviction of the earliest adopters.
The provenance (still owned by the first community member)
and out-sized price, created a feedback loop of hype and
treasury growth – fueling “ambitious” proposals from day
one. The treasury’s instant wealth (over $2M from Noun
1 alone) reinforced the community’s belief in “Nounish”
collective value, encouraging more participants to join and
further propagate Nounish memes and lore. Not unlike

Lil Nouns, the treasury attracted many proposals seeking
financial returns beyond the proposer’s wildest dreams,
many falling short and many just outright extraction from
the very community they claimed to love so much. The core
believers and community members can still be found to
this day, and the protocol has shown resilience unlike any
traditional company or entity. The largest extraction would
likely be Fork 0 where a mix of honest actors and arbitrage
opportunists left with half the treasury.
Xaix was understandably not happy about the fork
mechanism implemented into the protocol that leveraged
a huge arbitrage opportunity. In the end, around half of
the Nouns circulating supply decided to exit in Fork 0 at
a ~36ETH reimbursement per each Noun. A couple Forks
later and the DAO transitioned from Cayman Islands
Foundation wrapper to a Wyoming DUNA feat. KYC/AML
and No Forks Allowed.

In “The Selfish Gene,” Richard Dawkins introduced the concept
of the meme as a unit of cultural transmission, akin to a gene in
biological evolution. A successful meme replicates by capturing
attention, resonating emotionally, and encouraging imitation, thereby
embedding itself within the cultural fabric of spacetime. The advent
of blockchains has led to persisting/tokenizing these transmissions
and the formation of digital networks surrounding them.
Decentralized societies exist online in many forms, some powered by
these tokenized memes. Lil Nouns and Nouns are emergent cultural
arms of the Ethereum network. Nounish DAOs are unique in the
concept of infinite supply and no rarity - and a masterful simplicity
in design. Overly rigid hierarchies fail when the environment
becomes complex, because they lack requisite variety to absorb
change. Rather than relying on top-down control, Nounish DAOs use
open coordination and memetic signaling to create an emergent order
shaped by shared values, symbols, transparency, and iteration.
Q: What is a good meme?
A:

MEME VALUE
1) What
Memes that are more prevalent in Nounish tokennative communities, persisting for long periods of time,
culturally adopted, could be seen as high value.
Memetic value, the cultural significance and viral
potential of a concept, image, sound, riff, poem, design,
application, phrase, token etc, is measured by how well
it spreads within a community, with minimal mutation,
often through humor or relatable content. Mutation is
interesting in these open systems, and public domain
encourages mutation and simplification, thus speeding
up evolution, so perhaps this book departs from
Dawkins in one crucial way: mutation is not noise but
signal. Value is based on the meme’s ability to engage,
resonate, and foster a sense of belonging amongst
individuals. Value may be a discussion, proposal, vote,
new artwork by a specific token holder, or concept that
has resonated across the community.
Each block, transaction, proposal and token now
becomes a memetic marker, contextualized by the
genesis transaction and any events that follow, etched
into, in this case, Ethereum. We expect Ethereum
to persist long beyond our lifetimes, so you could
consider every onchain action and proposal as a
cultural landmark and/or reference point that you can
point back to from the future.
I naturally found myself drawn to a time known as
Noun o’clock (noc). Just as the sun rises each day,
blessing the world with light and energy, noc is the
time at which the protocol generates a new piece of
art (every ~24hrs at Nouns DAO, every ~12secs at
Lil Nouns DAO), thus allowing a new member to
join in exchange for adding ETH (the native token of
Ethereum) to the DAO treasury. Thus I am treating noc
as the ultimate source of the Nounish meme.

THE FRONTIER
Nouns exemplifies a rich memeplex: a complex, composable system
of memes that thrives on diversity and competition for attention.
Each meme entering this ecosystem contributes to its overall variety,
strengthening the community’s adaptability, resilience, and shared
lore. Participation is not passive. By collecting Nounish NFTs and
engaging in governance, individuals actively shape (and, most
importantly, are shaped by) an evolving cultural landscape.
Nounish DAOs represent the realization of long-standing cybernetic
aspirations. They embody principles of self-organization, feedback
loops, and decentralized control within a digital environment. DAOs
are not merely organizational tools but living systems capable
of cultural self-regulation. Understanding the interplay between
cybernetics and memetics offers insight into how ideas propagate,
stabilize, and evolve without centralized authority.
By becoming part of Nounish DAOs, participants immerse
themselves in a system where variety and feedback are the primary
drivers of cultural evolution. Ideas are proposed, tested, accepted,
rejected, remixed, and reintroduced. What persists does so not by
mandate, but through resonance and replication.
As a designer, I have chosen to focus my practice on the following
areas, outlined throughout this book, in no particular order:
a) pursuing creative design projects
b) promoting a gift economy
c) studying cybernetics
d) emphasizing noc
Historically, access to capital has been one of the greatest constraints
on creative and experimental work. Crowdfunding platforms such
as Kickstarter introduced an early feedback mechanism, allowing
creators to gauge public interest and adapt projects in real-time. This
decentralized signal enabled ideas outside the scope of traditional
venture capital to find support.
In parallel, Bitcoin demonstrated the viability of decentralized
financial networks, while Ethereum’s introduction of smart contracts
enabled a new generation of trust-minimized coordination. Smart
contracts automated execution and accountability, removing the need
for centralized intermediaries and unlocking novel forms of collective
funding and governance.
By 2025, these technologies have undergone multiple cycles of
hype, failure, recovery, and reinvention. Many projects collapsed
under their own complexity or misaligned incentives. Yet, much like
resilient cybernetic systems, a small number of products, protocols,
and platforms endured. They survived by adapting, continually
reconfiguring themselves in response to environmental pressures,
cultural shifts, and user behavior.
Nouns exists at this frontier: not as a static artwork or financial
instrument, but as an adaptive cultural system, one that remains alive
precisely because it can change.

Nouns DAO and Lil Nouns DAO are interactive at nearly
every level. These projects explicitly invite the community
to introduce new memes and elements that shift culture
and modify the collection forever. In this sense, authorship
is not closed but ongoing.
This stands in stark contrast to collections such as
Cryptopunks (est. 2017), widely regarded as pioneers of
digital art and NFTs, whose artwork is irrevocably locked
and capped at a fixed supply of 10,000. While historically
significant, such collections are fundamentally static.
Nouns, by comparison, treats art as a living system rather
than a finished product.
Interactivity, in my view, is the key property that makes
Nouns infinitely more compelling than anything else in
the NFT space. The difference is analogous to passively
consuming Netflix versus actively participating in a shared
world-building exercise. Nouns is not merely an art project
or an NFT-native meme; it is an interactive, self-regulating
cybernetic system.
In cybernetics, a system is commonly described as
comprising two interrelated subsystems:
Controller (C): the component that senses, evaluates, and
acts, comparing current states to desired goals and issuing
corrective actions.
Controlled system (S): the component whose behavior is
being regulated or guided by the controller.
The controller continuously monitors the state of the
system through feedback and adjusts inputs to steer the
system toward preferred outcomes. Crucially, it must
possess sufficient variety, that is, a broad enough range
of possible responses, to cope with the complexity and
disturbances presented by the controlled system.
I believe that many of the challenges Nouns DAO and Lil
Nouns DAO have faced historically, and continue to face,
are fundamentally variety problems. These issues arise
not from an excess of participation, but from insufficient
diversity of engagement within a relatively small and often
apathetic community. When the controller lacks variety, it
cannot adequately respond to changing conditions, cultural
drift, or coordination breakdowns.
The Nounish process, applicable to both Nouns DAO and
Lil Nouns DAO, is inherently recursive. Proposals lead
to votes; votes shape memes; memes influence future
proposals, bidding behavior, and participation patterns.
This feedback loop constitutes a form of self-organization.
In cybernetic terms, this dynamic closely resembles
Ashby’s Homeostat: an adaptive system that maintains
stability not by rigid control, but by continuously
reconfiguring itself in response to disturbances. Nouns
does not seek equilibrium through stasis, but through
ongoing cultural and structural adaptation.
How do I know I am not a variety attenuator?
I don’t, conclusively. I can only observe my own interventions. I attempted to increase
controller variety by opening governance bodies to many independent voices. Participation
failed. Attention consolidated elsewhere. Decision-making collapsed back into a smaller set
of actors, some voting with delegated power and minimal exposure to consequences. At that
point, decentralization became performative. I chose a different constraint: to privilege
the ritual itself over my own discretion. By binding my actions to noc as a forcing function,
opposing proposals that did not clearly engage or extend the ritual, I reduced my degrees
of freedom rather than expanded them. This does not eliminate attenuation, but it makes
it legible. When influence is exercised, it is exercised in service of a shared cadence, not
personal preference. If this too hardens, it must be dismantled.

Our onchain culture prizes individual freedom
but collective systems can’t yet sustain that level
of variety. When the diversity of actions outpaces
the system’s ability to absorb it, DAOs respond by
structuring themselves to cope. In cybernetic terms,
we reduce environmental variety to match the
DAO’s regulatory capacity. A DAO cannot possibly
provide requisite variety for each contributor or
proposer; it must generalize. The fantasy of a oneto-one steward for every member collapses the
collective under its own administrative weight.
Matching infinite personal variety is impossible
so we comply with Ashby’s Law through variety
attenuation. When the variety of individual
behaviors outpaces a system’s capacity to absorb
them, the system compensates through attenuation
thus reducing diversity to preserve stability.
This process is central to Stafford Beer’s Viable
System Model (VSM). According to Beer, every
viable organization must balance two flows:
variety generated by the environment and variety
absorbed through internal regulation. When
the environment’s variety exceeds what the
organization can handle, it must constrain, simplify,
or delay responses. In DAOs, this manifests as
governance processes, quorum requirements, and
proposal pipelines.
In this model, cost is not merely the money
required to achieve a goal. Cost is the total system
resource devoted to maintaining viability within
a given organizational framework; and when that
framework is maladaptive, and the relaxation time
(the delay between perturbation and response) is
too long, more and more resources are poured into
propping it up. The system then becomes selfreferentially expensive: it funds its own delay.
Governments and DAOs alike often fall into this
trap, endlessly “feeding the framework” to avoid
collapse, while making instability more likely.
Builder DAO is a useful case study in attenuation
via governance proliferation. More actors seeking
stability can paradoxically increase systemic
chaos. The proliferation of governance proposals,
compensations, and role definitions can flood a
DAO with noise rather than stability.

Platform for Change
In Platform for Change (1975), Beer uses the vivid
metaphor of “shooting the cat that’s hitting the ball” to
describe how organizations often respond to unpredictable
but non-destructive behavior by removing the source of
disturbance rather than redesigning the system to absorb it.
In banking, this principle manifests in risk management.
For instance, during the 2008 financial crisis, many banks
responded to volatility by eliminating traders and products
perceived as anomalous rather than redesigning incentive
structures or feedback systems that had amplified risk in
the first place. The system’s regulatory apparatus preferred
removal over adaptation. Instead of integrating the signal
that the market had become too tightly coupled, institutions
“shot the cat” by freezing credit lines, shutting down entire
divisions, or banning certain instruments (like CDOs),
thereby restoring apparent order at the cost of adaptive
intelligence. The noise (individual initiative, innovation)
was suppressed to protect the appearance of control.
In a DAO like Lil Nouns, proposals emerge from a
wide range of participants, many of whom operate with
divergent cultural norms, languages, creative styles, or
operational speeds. When this diversity produces friction
with controversial proposals, unorthodox funding requests,
overseas projects, the DAO usually responds not by
adjusting its process, but by suppressing the anomaly. The
reality at Lil Nouns is that just a handful of people decide
the fate of proposals, and it could be as little as a single
individual, such as the founder who controls a huge number
of votes. In contrast, Nouns DAO founders have essentially
stopped proposing to the DAO and sold large amounts of
their token allocation. The largest voting blocks at Nouns
could also pass a proposal alone, as at Lil Nouns, but these
were purchased tokens vs founder allocated. Still important
to remember that controller variety is not headcount; it is
independence of action, therefore having many aligned cofounders does not increase controller variety.
If DAOs are to mature as viable systems, they must move
beyond reflexive variety suppression. The challenge for
DAOs is to turn attenuation into intelligence and to regulate
not by exclusion, but by evolution.

n language, a noun is a person, place, or thing – a category of being. But cognitive linguistics teaches us that
categories aren’t rigid boxes; they’re fluid, dynamic groupings defined by prototypes and experiences. Eleanor
Rosch’s Prototype Theory showed that we categorize not by strict definitions but by family resemblances and
best examples. Imagine a “bird”, maybe a sparrow or robin comes to mind, or maybe a toucan or pelican - our
prototypes. A penguin, while biologically a bird, feels like an oddball because they stray from the prototype. The
category bird has fuzzy edges; some members are birdier than others. Like, say, what Nouns has become. “Noun”
started as a pixelated character with glasses, auctioned daily. But over time, “Noun” has grown to encompass an
ethos, a style, a community, a verb (“nounify”), adjective (“nounish”), a memeplex. Our understanding of Nouns
is prototype-based, not rule-based – it evolves as we create and encounter new examples. In the early days, perhaps
the prototype of a Noun was just the NFT itself. But soon the community became the prototype. Today, when we say
something is “Nounish,” we invoke a vibe more than a specific object. Does it embrace open-source creativity? Is
it a bit absurd or meme-worthy yet positive in spirit? Does it contribute to public good or fun? Does it challenge the
sq? These qualities have become the core of nounishness, our prototype for what fits in this world. Yet, importantly,
the boundaries remain fuzzy. A project putting Noun glasses on a giant pineapple statue could be nounish. So
could a Nouns-funded charity drive, or a musical, or a developer hackathon. We’ve learned to be comfortable
with ambiguity: just as a tomato can be a fruit or a vegetable depending on which prototype you compare it to, a
new idea can be part of Nouns even if it looks nothing like previous ones. This flexibility is a strength. It means the
Nouns community can continuously redefine itself without breaking – we’re not held back by a narrow definition
of what “belongs.” Embracing Prototype Theory in our community also guards us against dogma. We have a
loose constellation of values and iconic symbols and community members that serve as our guiding prototype.
This keeps us adaptive. When someone proposes something totally outlandish – say, funding a Nouns Molière
satirical theatre – our question isn’t “Does this meet a strict list of criteria?” but rather “Does it share enough
family resemblance with what we care about?” And if yes, we can stretch the category to include it. Over time,
some things will become central (prototypical) to Nouns and others will remain fringe – and that’s okay. The key is
that Nouns as a concept stays alive, growing and shifting. By understanding Nouns as a dynamic category, we give
ourselves permission to experiment wildly without losing our identity. We recognize that the center of nounishness
– things like open collaboration, whimsy, public good – stays solid even as the edges are constantly explored. This
cognitive flexibility has been crucial: it means Nouns can be a platform for imagination. We aren’t confined to one
art style, one use-case, or one narrative. Like language itself, we can invent new “words” (projects, memes, subcults) and see if they catch on. And as long as they resonate with the prototype – the core spirit – they become part
of the Nouns story. In short, Nouns is not a static noun at all; it’s an ongoing verb, a living process of redefinition.
Molière is nounish and I think this proposal would serve as a great prototype. This will create ongoing discussion
within, and around, traditional cultural institutions about innovative funding methods - specifically Ethereum and
Nouns. It presents a novel approach for 2Lang and similar entities to engage in the arts and offers patrons a new
avenue for support. tl;dr Nouns have fuzzy edges
